name: apple-hig
description: Use when designing, implementing, or reviewing interfaces for iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, watchOS, CarPlay, or other Apple system experiences using Apple's Human Interface Guidelines. Routes to current platform, foundation, pattern, component, input, and technology guidance.

# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

| Task | Read this topic skill |
|---|---|
| Platform conventions, design principles, games, device adaptation | [Getting started](subskills/apple-hig-getting-started/SKILL.md) |
| Accessibility, typography, color, materials, layout, localization, privacy | [Foundations](subskills/apple-hig-foundations/SKILL.md) |
| Onboarding, loading, search, sharing, accounts, feedback, media, settings | [Patterns](subskills/apple-hig-patterns/SKILL.md) |

| Buttons, menus, toolbars, menu bar, ornaments and actions | [Menus and actions](subskills/apple-hig-menus-and-actions/SKILL.md) |
| Sidebars, tab bars, search fields, tokens and path controls | [Navigation and search](subskills/apple-hig-navigation-and-search/SKILL.md) |
| Alerts, sheets, popovers, panels, scrolling and windows | [Presentation](subskills/apple-hig-presentation/SKILL.md) |
| Text fields, pickers, sliders, toggles, selection controls | [Selection and input](subskills/apple-hig-selection-and-input/SKILL.md) |
| Progress, activity, gauges and ratings | [Status](subskills/apple-hig-status/SKILL.md) |
| Widgets, Live Activities, notifications, Siri snippets and system surfaces | [System experiences](subskills/apple-hig-system-experiences/SKILL.md) |

| Apple Pay, purchases, Siri, VoiceOver, AI, CarPlay and integrations | [Technologies](subskills/apple-hig-technologies/SKILL.md) |

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;
`in-app-purchase` resolves to Apple In-App Purchase. The old Touch Bar and Messages
for Business HIG pages were unavailable at this snapshot. Do not fabricate their
current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

# Apple HIG: End-to-end behavior and recovery

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Trace the person’s task from entry through completion, cancellation, interruption and recovery. Select the pattern procedure for the actual failure or desired behavior before selecting its controls.
2. Preserve the current work, selection and navigation context across the transitions that matter. Choose interruption or modality according to urgency and task scope, not visual emphasis.
3. For asynchronous or recurring work, separate current progress, eventual result, error recovery and unavailable capability. For audio/video/haptics, specify user control and environmental behavior.
4. Deliver a transition/state specification, a correction to the supplied flow, or ranked findings tied to observed steps. Test alternate exits and resumption, not just the success path.

## Enter the topic procedure

Read the selected topic’s SKILL.md before its supporting guidance. For a review,
inspect actual evidence and return findings; for an implementation request, make
the authorized change; for design or adaptation, produce a usable specification
or patch. Load related topics only when the chosen procedure calls for them.

name: apple-hig-collaboration-and-sharing
description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting send-a-copy, collaborative sharing, participant permissions, management, and related updates.

# Separate sharing a copy from sharing access

Read [the collaboration guide](../../references/collaboration-and-sharing.md). This workflow is application advice; integration capability depends on infrastructure and platform.

Inspect object identity, sharing backend, participant/permission model, current UI, platform, and create/review/adapt intent. Distinguish copy transfer, ongoing collaboration, and synchronous SharePlay. Record existing access/link behavior; a Share button does not prove permissions or universal links work.

Use convenient standard Share entry/presentation and offer send-a-copy alongside collaboration. Explain a small logical set of who can access/edit/add participants. Once shared, expose Collaboration prominently with participants/communication, essential custom information, and management. Use system management where supplied; custom infrastructure needs appropriate representations, management UI, and universal links. Route updates to the relevant object rather than generic home. On visionOS explain that entering Full Space pauses Shared Space window streaming; on watch use supported ShareLink behavior. Do not claim this collaboration integration on tvOS.

Implement the authorized sharing UI/links/permission binding, specify access/representation/management contracts, or review concrete misleading-access defects. Do not actually send invitations or change live permissions without authorization; a design/build request can be satisfied with reviewable artifacts.

**Worked transformation:** Before: “Share” silently grants edit access to anyone with a link and offers no copy or management route. Decision: access and transfer have different consequences. After: expose explicit collaboration/copy choice, concise access/edit permissions, and a persistent Collaboration management route tied to the shared document.

Deliver the artifact, copy-versus-access model, permissions, participant management, and link destinations. Verify recipient scope, changed/revoked access, copied representation, and update links. Fail for access broader than described, copy mistaken for collaboration, or management unavailable after sharing. Separate mocked UI from actual backend enforcement/device integration.

Load [activity-views](../../../apple-hig-menus-and-actions/.topics/apple-hig-activity-views/SKILL.md) for share mechanics or [privacy](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-privacy/SKILL.md) for exposure decisions.

# Collaboration and sharing Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/collaboration-and-sharing) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. System sharing and Messages integrations can start collaboration and support communication, permissions, and ongoing event updates. CloudKit, iCloud Drive, and custom infrastructure can participate; custom implementations also need universal links. SharePlay separately supports synchronous shared activities. ## Best practices Put Share somewhere convenient, typically the toolbar, and use the system share sheet/popover or ShareLink. Collaboration method and permission choices appear in the iOS 16 share sheet and in the iPadOS 16 and macOS 13 sharing popover. Support send-a-copy alongside collaboration: CloudKit supplies file plus collaboration object, iCloud Drive already supports it, and custom infrastructure includes a file or plain-text representation in its object. Summarize access/edit permissions briefly and offer a small logically grouped set of choices, including who can access, edit, or add participants. Show Collaboration prominently when sharing starts, preferably next to Share. Its popover has participants/communication at top, optional custom actions in the middle, and management at bottom. Add only essential custom content, such as recent changes. Customize Manage Shared File wording where useful; CloudKit supplies management UI, while other implementations create it. Messages event notifications can report changes, mentions, joins, or departures with a universal link to the relevant app view. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, or macOS rules are specified. This collaboration integration is unavailable in tvOS. ### visionOS Shared Space screen sharing streams the current window. Entering Full Space pauses the stream for others until the app returns to Shared Space. ### watchOS SwiftUI ShareLink presents the system sharing interface. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Activity views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/activity-views) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI #### Videos ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, September 14, 2022.

# Apple HIG: Commands, roles and discoverable surfaces

Use this family to select and compose topic procedures. Infer the platform and
requested work from the supplied project; preserve its framework and constraints.

## Work through the decision

1. Inventory each command’s outcome, scope, availability and reversibility. Distinguish immediate commands from persistent selection before entering Buttons, Toggles, or the appropriate menu procedure.
2. Choose a discoverable primary surface plus contextual shortcuts. On Mac, consider the menu bar’s command catalog and keyboard access even when a toolbar or context menu also exposes the action.
3. Use consequence and current task to decide role/default, confirmation and recovery. Consult Alerts and Undo and redo when that decision depends on destructive behavior; preserve documented exceptions.
4. Deliver an action contract naming labels, roles, surfaces, shortcuts, availability and relevant pending/resolved behavior. Verify the action and its recovery rather than color alone.

# Share the current content through its context

Read [the activity-view guide](../../references/activity-views.md). The procedure is application advice; distinguish activity views from Mac share/action extensions.

Inspect the content types, selection, Share entry point, target platform, and create/review/adapt request. Determine whether a proposed extension transfers information elsewhere or acts on it in context. Record available content and current task eligibility; do not assume every system destination supports every payload.

Use the standard Share button and system presentation where supported. Offer only relevant custom activities, avoid duplicate system actions, and name specialized variants distinctly with concise verbs. Do not prescribe system task order, which the app cannot control. Choose a familiar composition view; if custom UI is necessary keep it short and related to the host app. An extension is already modal, so avoid another modal except a necessary alert.

Implement the share payload/activities, deliver a payload-to-destination/action specification, or review exact relevance and handoff failures. If work continues after dismissal, specify background continuation and status in the main app; notify for problems rather than routine completion. On Mac use supported share/action extension entry points without claiming a Mac activity-view component; tvOS/watchOS lack activity views.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a document share sheet adds branded `Acme Print`, duplicates Print, and closes only after a large upload finishes. Decision: the custom action is redundant and long work should not trap the extension. After: retain system Print, name the distinct transfer `Send for Approval`, dismiss after accepting the task, and surface its status/problem in the app.

Deliver the artifact plus payload, custom eligibility, dismissal, and continuation contract. Verify with the actual selected content, unavailable destinations, cancellation, and post-dismissal work. Fail for missing payload, duplicate misleading actions, nested modal traps, or claimed ordering control. Separate extension execution from inspected specification.

Load [collaboration-and-sharing](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-collaboration-and-sharing/SKILL.md) for permissions or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for extension exits.

# Activity views Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/activity-views) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. The system share sheet offers contextual sharing, common actions, and frequently used apps. It appears as a sheet or popover according to device and orientation. App-specific activities normally precede general system actions; people can customize the action list. Extensions can expose share/action functionality in other apps, including on macOS even though Mac has no activity-view component. ## Best practices Use the standard Share button to reveal it. Exclude irrelevant tasks and show only currently appropriate custom tasks; system task order is not app-controlled. Avoid duplicating existing actions such as Print. Give a specialized variation a clearly distinct name. Use a short verb phrase for custom actions without product/company branding; share destinations can use the company name beneath their icon. Prefer SF Symbols; center a custom glyph in an approximately 70×70-pixel area. ## Share and action extensions Share extensions transfer contextual information to another app or service; action extensions operate on content without leaving context. iOS/iPadOS expose both through the share sheet. On Mac, sharing comes from toolbar or context-menu Share; actions may come from embedded-content controls, a toolbar, or Finder quick actions. Prefer the familiar system composition view for sharing. Include the app name for an action extension and use related app interface elements when a custom UI is necessary. Keep the task to few steps. Avoid stacking another modal over the already modal extension, except a necessary alert. Share extensions inherit the app icon; actions should use a meaningful symbol or glyph. Continue long work in the background after dismissal and show status in the main app. Notify only about a problem rather than routine completion. ## Platform considerations No additional iOS, iPadOS, or visionOS rules are specified. Activity views themselves are unsupported in macOS, tvOS, and watchOS; Mac share/action extensions remain supported as described above. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) [Popovers](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/popovers) #### Developer documentation — UIKit — UIKit — Foundation #### Videos

# Ask for precise access when its purpose is clear

Read [Privacy](../../references/privacy.md). Inspect the feature's actual data needs, transfers, storage, current permission flow, and supported platform. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode. Produce the requested copy/flow/data-handling changes in the existing stack; distinguish documented platform restrictions from additional application recommendations.

Map each requested category to a specific feature and minimum necessary scope. Remove collection without a concrete benefit; prefer on-device work where it avoids unnecessary transfer. Explain collection/use accurately and flag App Store disclosure updates needed when behavior changes. Respect private email and tracking choices rather than designing around them.

Ask when the person invokes the feature. Launch-time requests need an essential, obvious dependency. Write a short active purpose sentence explaining use and reason. If context is sufficient, omit a custom pre-alert; if explanation is essential, use one clear continuation to the real system alert without imitating Allow/Don't Allow. Keep the guide's special pre-alert restrictions distinct from ordinary onboarding. Tracking requires its system authorization before collection and must not be incentivized or manipulated.

Choose one-time location access for suitable individual tasks using the system location button on supported platforms; preserve permitted customization and all localized/accessibility-sized text. Protect secrets with established authentication/keychain mechanisms. For Mac, account for sandboxing/distribution and fast user switching. For visionOS, separate system rendering assistance from permission-gated Full Space ARKit data; gaze remains private, and imported phone-camera assumptions may need removal or content import.

**Before → decision → after:** A bird journal asks for contacts, microphone, and continuous location at launch although only “Attach current location” uses location. Decision: request only the specific action's needed access. After, journaling works immediately; the attachment action offers the supported location control, and its purpose explains adding the sighting's location.

Deliver a data-purpose/access matrix and corrected permission sequence/copy or implementation. Fail if collection precedes required consent, copy obscures the real use, or unrelated work is gated on optional access. Report code/flow evidence separately from actual authorization prompts and privacy-setting behavior; this procedure does not certify security or legal compliance.

Use [Sign in with Apple](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-sign-in-with-apple/SKILL.md) for that authentication choice and [Augmented reality](../../../apple-hig-technologies/.topics/apple-hig-augmented-reality/SKILL.md) when room/camera access is essential.

# Privacy Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) · Retrieved 2026-10-25. This is original application guidance based on the source text. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. Communicate collection and usage clearly and protect granted data. Keep App Store privacy disclosures accurate for new releases and updates; people rely on them before downloading. ## Best practices Collect only what the specific feature requires and make access as precise as possible. Respect Hide My Email, Mail Privacy Protection, and tracking choices. Prefer on-device processing, including Create ML/Neural Engine where useful, to avoid unnecessary server transfers. Use system encryption, key management, and established security protections, including CloudKit’s additional encrypted data types where available. ## Requesting permission Protected categories include personal/location/health/financial/contact information, user-created content, messages/calendar/music/gameplay/HomeKit data, media, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/local network resources, camera/microphone, the advertising identifier, and permission-gated ARKit data in a visionOS Full Space. The system displays the app’s purpose string and stores choices/descriptions in privacy settings. Ask when the person invokes the relevant feature. Request at launch only when access is essential and obviously necessary, such as location for navigation or room information for a spatial game that needs walls. Write a short, specific, active, complete sentence in sentence case with a period, explaining both use and reason. Vague promises of a better experience and commands to enable access do not explain the need. ### Pre-alert screens, windows, or views Usually context explains the request. If extra explanation is essential, use one button clearly leading to the system alert, such as Continue/Next; do not label it Allow or mimic the actual consent choice. Do not add cancellation, close, or other actions except those needed for legal consent. These restrictions apply to pre-permission custom explanations, not ordinary unrelated onboarding screens. ### Tracking requests Show the AppTrackingTransparency alert before collecting tracking information, including if tracking begins at launch. Do not offer incentives, imitate a permission prompt, display an image of the alert, annotate behind it, or otherwise manipulate rushed choices. Such patterns can cause App Review rejection. A legally required consent view before/after the system alert is permitted by the source’s stated review guidance. ## Location button On iOS/iPadOS/watchOS, the system location button provides one-time access at the task’s moment of need. The first tap teaches and confirms its behavior through a system alert; later taps grant access without repeating that education. Authorization expires when app use ends. With no prior status it resembles Allow Once; an existing While Using status is unchanged. Use it for individual tasks such as attaching a location or finding a nearby item/store. Customize only the supplied title, filled/outline glyph, foreground/background colors, and corner radius. Keep all localized and accessibility-size text untruncated and maintain contrast/transparency limits. Persistent customization violations can prevent location access even though the button still triggers other app actions. ## Protecting data Prefer passkeys; if passwords remain, add two-factor verification. Use Face ID, Optic ID, or Touch ID to protect continued signed-in access where appropriate. Store secrets in the encrypted keychain, never plaintext files even with restrictive permissions. Prefer established authentication, Sign in with Apple, and Password AutoFill over invented schemes. ## Platform considerations No extra iOS/iPadOS/tvOS/watchOS rules are listed. ### macOS Sign externally distributed apps with a valid Developer ID. Use sandboxing to limit resource/data access; Mac App Store apps require it. Account for fast user switching rather than assuming the current person is the only signed-in account. ### visionOS System ARKit algorithms support lighting, mapping, persistence, segmentation, and related rendering in Shared Space without exposing raw data to apps. ARKit API access requires Full Space, and plane estimation, scene reconstruction, image anchoring, and hand tracking require permission. Gaze remains private: system hover feedback can respond before a tap without disclosing where someone looks. Compatibility back-camera input is blank; front-camera input represents spatial Personas with permission. Adapt imported phone/tablet camera-dependent features by removal or content import instead of assuming conventional camera capture. ## Resources Consult the [official article](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy) for linked Apple design assets and implementation resources. #### Related The official article links the adjacent HIG topics relevant to this guidance. #### Developer documentation Use the framework references linked by Apple for current API availability and implementation details. #### Videos Apple’s linked design sessions provide demonstrations and additional implementation context; no video review is implied here. ## Change log Source revision dates: June 21, 2023.

name: apple-hig-buttons
description: Use when designing, reviewing, or adapting action buttons, including their labels, roles, emphasis, hit regions, and platform behavior.

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.
5. Only when the command has delayed completion, define the initiating, waiting, and resolved behavior. On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Specify how duplicate activation is handled and what success or failure means in the product; do not promise network completion from a press animation.

Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. For adaptation, map each affected control to its destination platform rather than copying appearance alone.

## Deliver and verify

Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. Fail the design if a destructive consequence is mislabeled, peer targets overlap, an icon has no discoverable name, or custom press feedback is absent. State separately which checks were inspected in source, exercised, or remain Apple-device checks; Linux inspection does not prove gaze, VoiceOver, haptics, or native rendering.

## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

**After:** Specify `Export…` as the prominent action opening export settings, `Remove Photos` as a lower-emphasis command with a visible Undo path, and `Done` for finishing metadata edits. Inspect actual save semantics before changing `Close` to `Done`. Verify the Return mapping, undo restoration, and that each accessible name matches the resulting action. These product choices are an example application, not facts about the unseen implementation.

## Conditional handoffs

Load alerts for consequential confirmation/default decisions; toggles or segmented-controls for persistent selection; pop-up-buttons or pull-down-buttons for menu-opening behavior; toolbars when placement belongs to window chrome; and accessibility when naming, focus, contrast, or target access needs deeper work. Keep this button contract as the input to the next topic.

# Buttons Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. ## Contents - [Best practices](#Best-practices) - [Style](#Style) - [Content](#Content) - [Role](#Role) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) A button performs an immediate action. Its visual style, visible symbol/text, and semantic role work together to explain what activation does. ## Best practices Allow enough surrounding space for clear separation and easy selection. General hit regions should be at least 44×44 pt; visionOS targets need 60×60 pt. Custom buttons always need press feedback. ## Style Prefer system styles for built-in states, accessibility, and appearance adaptation. Use one or two prominent buttons per view for likely actions. Distinguish a preferred option through style rather than making related buttons different sizes. Keep label colors distinct from colorful content; the default monochrome often works best over rich backgrounds. ## Content Use a familiar symbol for a familiar action; use a short title-case verb phrase when words are clearer. Mac and visionOS can provide brief hover tooltips; text-labeled buttons usually explain themselves. ## Role Normal has no special meaning; primary is the expected/default action; Cancel abandons the current action; destructive signals data loss. Roles affect rendering, such as accent fill for primary and red for destructive. Primary can respond to Return and close a temporary view. Generally assign primary only to a nondestructive likely action. Application advice: consult the alert-specific deliberate-destruction exception before prescribing confirmation behavior. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS For delayed completion, show an activity indicator within the activating button, optionally changing its label to the current operation. The indicator replaces any button image while preserving context for the wait. ### macOS #### Push buttons The standard push button can show text, imagery, or both and can serve as default. Use flexible height for tall icons or multiple text lines, otherwise retain standard sizing. Append an ellipsis when the button opens another window/view/app for further input. Consider spring loading through a dragged selection plus force-click on Magic Trackpad, preserving the drag afterward. #### Square buttons These small glyph-only controls affect a nearby view, for example adding/removing table rows. They can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls. Use them in the body rather than the frame, toolbar, or status bar. Prefer system symbols and omit introductory labels when proximity explains the function. #### Help buttons Use the familiar system question-mark control, at most one per window, opening context-specific help when possible and top-level help otherwise. In a dialog with dismissal controls, place it in the opposite lower corner, aligned vertically with those controls. Without dismissal controls, or in settings, use either lower corner. Keep it in the view body and omit explanatory introductory text. #### Image buttons Image buttons can act as push, toggle, or pop-up controls inside a view. Toolbar imagery instead belongs to a toolbar item. Allow about 10 pixels between image and clickable button edges and generally omit a visible system border. Put any needed label beneath the image. ### visionOS Buttons normally have a visible background and audible feedback. Circle suits glyph-only content, rounded rectangle or capsule suits text, and capsule suits text plus glyph. Standard states supply feedback; custom hover effects are not supported. A look-triggered tooltip can explain a glyph. | Shape | Supported visual sizes | | --- | --- | | Circle | Mini 28 pt; small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt; extra large 64 pt | | Text capsule | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Text-and-icon capsule | Regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | | Rounded rectangle | Small 32 pt; regular 44 pt; large 52 pt | Visual size does not remove the 60-pt targeting requirement. Use a discernible shape/fill except inside a larger clearly bounded toolbar, menu, alert, or ornament. On window glass, thin material suits the button; floating in space, use glass. Reserve white fill with black content for the system's toggled state. Prefer round/capsule forms for steady gaze, and a capsule for a standalone button. Keep centers at least 60 pt apart; add 4 pt padding around buttons 60 pt or larger to prevent hover overlap. Avoid rows/stacks of mini/small buttons. Prefer rounded rectangles for vertical text stacks and capsules for horizontal rows. Standard sounds matter because visionOS provides no haptics. ### watchOS Inline buttons are capsules with a contrasting material. Put corner actions in a toolbar so the system relocates title/time and gives controls Liquid Glass. Full-width buttons suit primary actions. Side-by-side buttons should share height and use short labels or glyphs; vertical one- and two-line buttons should also maintain common heights. Toolbar actions can navigate related areas or operate on current content. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Pop-up buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pop-up-buttons) [Pull-down buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pull-down-buttons) [Toggles](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/toggles) [Segmented controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/segmented-controls) [Location button](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/privacy#Location-button) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: December 16, 2025, June 9, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 21, 2023, June 5, 2023.

# Interrupt only for a decision that warrants it

Read [the alert guide](../../references/alerts.md). Apply the following as application advice and preserve the documented deliberate-destruction exception.

Inspect the triggering condition, urgency, reversibility, prior user intent, platform, and create/review/adapt request. Establish whether immediate attention is necessary. Do not turn every status update or startup network failure into an alert; ordinary undoable deletion can use recovery instead. Record evidence of the actual outcome and default-key behavior, not just button color.

Write a contextual neutral title and only useful supporting text; name outcomes instead of Yes/No. Use at most three buttons with meaningful roles and a safe Cancel beside destruction. Distinguish unexpected destructive consequences from confirmation of explicitly requested destruction: the latter may retain a normal default so Return confirms intent. Cancel is not the default; consider no default when deliberate reading is necessary. A single default completion acknowledgment should be Done, while OK can acknowledge purely informational content. Do not impose one platform's button geometry everywhere.

Implement the alert/handlers or deliver exact copy, role/default/order, trigger, and result specification; reviews must identify the specific misleading consequence or unnecessary interruption. Use fields only when resolution requires input and secure entry for passwords. Apply relevant platform accessory/cancellation rules: Mac suppression/Help only when useful, visionOS accessory limits and parent/space relationship, keyboard/remote alternate cancellation where supported. Post-action alternatives may belong in an action sheet.

**Worked transformation:** Before: an editor displays `Error 47` with OK/Cancel after an unrequested operation would overwrite unsaved work; Return commits overwrite. Decision: the consequence is unexpected and concealed. After: explain the conflicting draft, offer explicit safe recovery/cancellation and appropriately destructive replacement, and define a default that cannot accidentally accept unexplained loss.

Deliver the artifact and trigger/outcome/default contract. Verify Return, Cancel, supported escape, enlarged text, and repeated errors without stacked alerts. Fail for concealed loss, misleading action text, no safe cancellation, or routine status forcing interruption. Separate handler checks from native alert/assistive execution.

Use [action-sheets](../apple-hig-action-sheets/SKILL.md) for alternatives, [undo-and-redo](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-undo-and-redo/SKILL.md) for reversible work, or [modality](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-modality/SKILL.md) for surrounding exits.

# Alerts Source: [Apple Human Interface Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/alerts) Snapshot: 2026-10-25. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. An alert interrupts to communicate urgent, critical information and useful actions, including problems, unexpected data loss, or important confirmations. ## Best practices Reserve alerts for situations that warrant immediate attention. Put informational status in context when no action is required. Common undoable deletions generally need no confirmation; uncommon irreversible destruction does. Avoid startup alerts: cached or placeholder content with a discreet problem explanation is often a better response to an unavailable network. ## Anatomy Alerts are modal and adapt their appearance to iOS, iPadOS, macOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS rather than using one universal layout. ## Content Use a title, optional message, and up to three buttons. iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS can include text fields; macOS and visionOS can include an icon and accessory view. macOS additionally supports a suppression checkbox and Help button. Use direct, neutral, approachable wording without blaming the person or concealing severity. The title should explain what happened, its context, and cause as concisely as possible, generally within two lines. Avoid a bare error label or code. Complete-sentence titles use sentence case and punctuation; fragments use title case without punctuation. Additional text should add information in brief complete sentences. Clear action labels should make button explanations unnecessary; if instructions are unavoidable, use device-neutral language such as choose and the exact title without quotation marks. Include an input field only when resolving the situation requires it, with secure entry for passwords. ## Buttons Use short, usually one- or two-word, title-case action labels without punctuation. Prefer specific outcomes over Yes/No or ambiguous OK; reserve OK for purely informational acknowledgment. A cancellation action is always Cancel. Place the expected/default action at the trailing end of a row or top of a stack, with cancellation generally leading or at the bottom. Apply destructive styling to destructive consequences the person did not deliberately request. A confirmation of an explicitly chosen destruction, such as Empty Trash, can retain a normal default action so Return confirms intent. Always provide Cancel alongside destructive actions, but do not make Cancel the default. To force a deliberate reading, consider no default. A single default acknowledgment button should be Done rather than Cancel. Support familiar alternate cancellation where appropriate: Home Screen exit on iOS/iPadOS; Escape or Command-Period on attached keyboards in iOS/iPadOS/macOS/visionOS; Menu on the tvOS remote. ## Platform considerations No additional tvOS or watchOS rules are specified. ### iOS, iPadOS Use action sheets for multiple choices following an intentional action. Keep titles and optional messages short to minimize scrolling, while accommodating enlarged accessibility text. ### macOS The app icon appears automatically but can be replaced. Repeating alerts can offer suppression; necessary details can use an accessory view, and Help can open documentation. Reserve a caution symbol for situations needing extra attention, particularly unexpected loss, rather than routine overwrite, save, or empty-trash tasks. ### visionOS In Shared Space, an alert sits slightly in front of its parent window and stays attached when the window moves. In Full Space, it centers in the wearer's field of view. An accessory view must be no taller than 154 pt and use a 16-pt corner radius. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Modality](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/modality) [Action sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/action-sheets) [Sheets](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/sheets) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: February 2, 2024, September 12, 2023, June 21, 2023.
